text.text: Your chiropractic office on one page. Start with Inquiries to call back today, then Visits for the day's schedule, and keep an eye on Packages so nobody loses prepaid visits. Operational tracking only; clinical notes stay in your clinical system.
People call a chiropractor when something hurts. The office that calls back first, books soonest and sounds like it can help usually gets the patient.
with their name, phone, how they found you and the reason (low back, neck, headaches, sports injury, posture or wellness). Set
Call back within an hour during office hours. If you get voicemail, leave your name, the office and two times available today or tomorrow.
Text the same two times right after.
Ask what happened and when. Recent injuries from a fall or car accident need a different intake (auto claims, possible imaging).

Ask about red flags the doctor wants to hear about before booking: numbness in both legs, loss of bladder or bowel control, severe unexplained pain, recent major trauma. Those callers are referred to urgent care or the emergency room; write that down on the inquiry.
Explain the first visit plainly: history, exam, X-rays if needed, a report of findings, and often a first adjustment.
Give the price of the first visit and whether you bill their insurance.
New patient exam booked within 48 hours
Intake forms sent by text or email

text.text: Leads from a screening get a call within two days while they still remember you. Mention the event by name.
"We can see you tomorrow at 7:30 before work, or 5:15 after. The first visit is about an hour, and Dr. Gideon will tell you at the end whether he thinks he can help."
once a month. If social posts bring wellness callers and patient referrals bring injury cases, plan your outreach around that.
Care plans give patients a clear path and the office steady income. They only work when the visits are tracked honestly and expiring plans are used, not forgotten.

(frequent visits for two to four weeks),

If they cannot use them in time, the office manager decides on an extension. Write the reason on the plan.
If a patient stops care, refund unused visits at the plan's per-visit price, less any discount they received for buying the plan. Put the policy in writing at the point of sale.
Harlan's ten-visit maintenance card shows an expiry date four days ago with visits left. The front desk calls, he books two visits next week, and the manager notes a two-week extension on the plan.

text.text: The first visit decides whether someone becomes a patient. The second visit, the report of findings, decides whether they follow a plan.
Intake forms returned: history, current medications, previous injuries and surgeries
Insurance checked if you bill it: chiropractic visit limit, copay, whether X-rays are covered
Prior imaging requested from their physician if it exists
Visit 1: history and exam (about an hour)
Check in, scan the ID and insurance card, collect the first-visit fee.
The doctor takes a history, does the orthopedic and neurological exam, and decides on X-rays.
If red flags appear, the doctor refers out and the visit ends there. Write it down.
Many offices give a first adjustment at this visit when it is safe to do so.
Book visit 2 within two days before the patient leaves.
Visit 2: report of findings (20 to 30 minutes)
The doctor explains what was found in plain words, shows the X-rays, and recommends a phase and a number of visits.
The front desk presents the matching care plan and payment options, then books the full first two weeks.

At each re-exam the doctor measures progress against the first visit and decides the next phase. Update
and set the next re-exam date. Patients in Wellness are re-examined every six months.
Zainab came in with headaches after a new desk job. Her exam was today at 4 pm; her report of findings is booked for Thursday. If she starts a Relief plan, her re-exam goes in for four weeks out.
